subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Working Scientifically: Data and Graph Skills Reading
subtitle: Reading practice for interpreting scientific data, graphs and conclusions.
description: A KS3 reading pack focused on data and graph skills in working scientifically. Passages cover variables, tables, graph choice, scales, anomalies, correlations, conclusions and evaluation.

data.sourcePassage: Scientific data is information collected from observations or measurements. A measurement is a value found using equipment, such as 24 degrees C, 50 g or 12 s. An observation is something noticed, such as a solution turning cloudy. Raw data is the original data recorded during an investigation. Processed data is data that has been changed into a more useful form, such as a mean or a graph. In an investigation, the independent variable is deliberately changed, the dependent variable is measured, and control variables are kept the same. For example, if a student tests how ramp height affects the distance a toy car travels, ramp height is the independent variable and distance travelled is the dependent variable. Keeping the same car and ramp surface helps make the test fair.

questions.question: What is scientific data?
questions.modelAnswer: Scientific data is information collected from observations or measurements.

questions.question: In the ramp investigation, which variable is deliberately changed?
questions.modelAnswer: Ramp height

questions.question: Why are control variables important in this investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: They help make the test fair by reducing the effect of other factors on the distance travelled.

questions.question: Which example is processed data?
options: A mean calculated from repeat times
questions.modelAnswer: A mean calculated from repeat times

questions.question: Explain why data alone is not enough for a strong scientific conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer: The data must be organised, processed, interpreted and linked to the investigation question before it can support a conclusion.

data.sourcePassage: A good results table makes data easier to check and understand. It should have a clear title, headings for variables, units in the headings, repeat measurements where needed, and a mean column when repeats are used. Units should not be repeated in every data cell. For example, a column heading should say Time taken (s), and the cells should contain values such as 12, 13 and 11. To calculate the mean, add the values and divide by the number of values. For 12 s, 13 s and 11 s, the mean is 36 divided by 3, which is 12 s. Repeats are useful because they help show whether results are consistent. A small range between repeat values suggests good repeatability, while a large range may show error, variation or poor control of variables.

questions.question: Where should units usually be placed in a results table?
questions.modelAnswer: Units should usually be placed in the column headings.

questions.question: What is the mean of 12 s, 13 s and 11 s?
Why should a table include repeat measurements when appropriate?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeat measurements help check whether the results are consistent and support judgements about repeatability.

questions.question: What might a large range between repeat readings suggest?
questions.modelAnswer: It may suggest measurement error, natural variation, poor control of variables or another problem with the method.

questions.question: Explain why putting units in every data cell can make a table weaker.
questions.modelAnswer: It makes the table cluttered and less clear; units in the heading show what all values in that column mean.

data.sourcePassage: The best graph type depends on the type of data and the purpose of the investigation. A bar chart is usually best for categoric data, such as comparing different surfaces or substances. Bars should have gaps because the categories are separate. A line graph is usually best when the independent variable is continuous and the investigation shows change, such as temperature over time or gas volume during a reaction. A scatter graph is used for paired measurements when looking for a relationship or correlation, such as hand span and reaction time. A pie chart is useful for showing parts of a whole, but it is rarely the best choice for showing how one variable affects another in an investigation. Choosing the wrong graph can make the data harder to interpret or even suggest the wrong kind of pattern.

questions.question: Which graph is best for comparing different surfaces?
questions.modelAnswer: Bar chart

questions.question: Why should bars have gaps in a bar chart for categoric data?
questions.modelAnswer: The gaps show that the categories are separate groups.

questions.question: Which graph is most suitable for temperature measured over time?
questions.modelAnswer: Line graph

questions.question: Why is a scatter graph suitable for hand span and reaction time?
questions.modelAnswer: Each student has a pair of measurements, and the graph can show whether there is a correlation between them.

questions.question: Explain why choosing the wrong graph can weaken a scientific answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The wrong graph can hide the pattern, make the data harder to read, or suggest a continuous relationship when the data is actually categoric.

data.sourcePassage: A graph scale is the set of value steps on an axis. Equal spaces on an axis must represent equal increases, otherwise the graph can be misleading. Good scales often use simple intervals such as 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 or 50. A graph does not always have to start at zero, but the scale must be clear and fair. Interpolation means estimating a value between measured points. For example, if water is 70 degrees C at 2 minutes and 62 degrees C at 4 minutes, the temperature at 3 minutes might be about 66 degrees C. Extrapolation means estimating beyond the measured data. It is less certain because the pattern may change outside the range tested. A strong trend description should use values and units, not just say that the graph goes up or down.

questions.question: What must equal spaces on an axis represent?
questions.modelAnswer: Equal spaces must represent equal increases.

questions.question: What is interpolation?
questions.modelAnswer: Estimating between measured points

questions.question: If water is 70 degrees C at 2 minutes and 62 degrees C at 4 minutes, what is a reasonable estimate at 3 minutes?
questions.modelAnswer: About 66 degrees C

questions.question: Why is extrapolation less certain than interpolation?
questions.modelAnswer: Extrapolation goes beyond the measured data, where the pattern may change and is not directly supported by results.

questions.question: Improve this weak trend description: 'The graph goes down.'
questions.modelAnswer: A stronger answer would describe the variables and quote values with units, such as: as time increased from 0 min to 10 min, temperature decreased from 80 degrees C to 50 degrees C.

data.sourcePassage: An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern or is very different from other repeat results. Anomalies should not automatically be removed. Scientists should first check whether there is evidence of a measurement error, equipment error, method error, uncontrolled variable or recording mistake. If there is a justified reason, the anomalous result may be excluded from a mean, but this decision must be explained. A strong conclusion answers the investigation question, describes the trend, uses numerical evidence with units and mentions limitations if relevant. Evaluation means judging the quality of the data and method. Accuracy means closeness to the true value, while precision can mean close repeat readings or small measurement intervals. Reliability is about trustworthiness and is improved by repeats, clear patterns and careful control of variables.

questions.question: What is an anomaly?
questions.modelAnswer: An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern or is very different from other repeat results.

questions.question: Which reason could justify excluding an anomalous result?
options: There was evidence of a method or measurement error
It made the graph look less neat
It made the conclusion harder to write
questions.modelAnswer: There was evidence of a method or measurement error

questions.question: What should a strong scientific conclusion include?
questions.modelAnswer: It should answer the question, describe the trend, use numerical evidence with units and mention limitations if relevant.

questions.question: Which word means closeness to the true value?
questions.modelAnswer: Accuracy

questions.question: Explain why reliable results are not always accurate.
questions.modelAnswer: Results can be consistent and repeatable but still wrong if the equipment is not calibrated correctly or the method has a systematic error.
